God's law would least of all choose to do wrong, thus let us consider what it means to change the plow into a sword and the sickle into a pruning hook, for the law seems to hint to us that the time has come for those justified and sanctified in Christ to wage war against passions and sins, not to be slow in fulfilling the better things, but to transform their efforts towards virtue, and to be strong in spiritual struggles, as Paul also exhorts us to stand firm in truth and righteousness, and to take up the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation

Wise, gentle, and kind to divine laws. Who would be those pursuing a life contrary to what I said, and thus being expelled from the holy multitude of saints? God himself explains to Moses. Command the Israelites to send away from the camp all lepers, those with gonorrhea, and all unclean people, so they do not defile their camps where God dwells. You hear that it is necessary to expel from the camp those with gonorrhea, lepers, and the unclean, lest they pollute others. What then? I would say that it is reasonable. It would be better for God, being the ruler of holiness and justice, to show mercy to those who have suffered unfortunate events, rather than punishing them. For leprosy, physical harm, and involuntary suffering happen to human bodies, but they are not considered sins.

He would rather choose, even if one of the wealthy is amazed, to give up all his property to those who promise to deliver him. Then how will the written law and the confession to the sick be? The miserable ways and the uncontrolled desire that is sick with shame and prefers the worse things would be punished. The things that do not have this nature, but happen to those who suffer unwillingly, would be pitied, and it seems that one should also pity the one who is reproached. What then do we say to these things? The law has wronged the lepers, or has it imposed a harsh punishment on others, not having pardoned the hunt that is fitting? Not at all, but it is necessary. For it is written: 'The law is holy, and the commandment is holy, and just, and good.' But how would this be understood by us, if someone were to ask? We say that the beauty of truth was shown through a type and a shadow in the commandment given through Moses to the ancients, and the power of the things hidden in the mind was clearly shown in the bodily weaknesses. For the written law resembles the lepers, as far as it has come to ways, many-formed and many-minded, and filled with various evils, having their own mind in themselves. It says that the one who is uncontrolled in lust is defiled, and is unconquerably defeated by excessive shame, as it seems to be a passion that endures the suffering of uncontrolled lust.

The unyielding sorrow is concealed within the soul, that is, the sorrow that has been taken on account of the dead and is deeply grieved. Not being unguarded, as if going, and almost dragging the word, we say that following the nature of the theories and seeing the innermost of the written, as inactive towards battle, and towards the necessary, being seen as worse than the passions, in no way being suitable, the multiform falls into wickedness, if some were to take it. For this is leprosy and the passion according to it. But neither would the unchaste and intemperate towards external pleasures be enrolled in the phalanx of the saints. Those who have excessively despised the dead are sent away. For contempt is a matter against God, although it has been cried out clearly through the voice of the saints: 'The dead will rise, and those in the tombs will be raised.' Let us therefore be manly, as is necessary, I say, to be seen as better than the passions. For thus someone will be enrolled among the accustomed to be well-approved; and being equal to those who have been perfectly examined, they will truly abandon the much-praised glory. Let not the pains frighten, even if the approach to the praised life seems rough; even if the path of virtue is difficult and contrary, the sweats of glory will appear beforehand. For it is not possible, it is not possible, for a few to easily despise the pains and to be able to abundantly possess the excellent achievements; but proportionally to the sweats, the things from them are also seen. Such people are exhorted by the divine Paul to strive for virtue.

For it is pleasing to make an outline, 'the author and finisher of our faith, Jesus, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising shame.' And in what way and for what things he bore the cross for us, emptying himself, being God by nature, the Word, let us say, briefly elevating the narrative, and usefully applying it to the so-called voluntary emptying. For the Son, who is in him and from him by nature, is born from God and Father effortlessly and beyond mind. Again, let us say, the mind goes beyond bodies; and leaving behind the insignificant fantasy about them, it is better by far to think of the divine as incomparable to the nature of the body; and it is more excellent to consider it as having the glory of all that is generated and unblemished. Let us accept, therefore, not necessarily following our own reasoning, that what is older than what is generated is that it does not exist at all; and somehow the non-existence appears before the transition into being.
pass_b_english: The law of God would not choose to do wrong, and so let us consider what it means to change the plow into a sword and the sickle into a pruning hook.

The law seems to hint to us that the time has come for those justified and sanctified in Christ to wage war against passions and sins, not to be slow in fulfilling the better things, but to transform their efforts towards virtue, and to be strong in spiritual struggles.
As the apostle Paul exhorts us, we must stand firm in truth and righteousness, and take up the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation.
The wise and gentle person is kind to divine laws.
However, there are those who pursue a life contrary to what has been said, and as a result, they are expelled from the holy multitude of saints.

God himself explains this to Moses, saying that the Israelites must send away from their camp all lepers, those with gonorrhea, and all unclean people, so they do not defile their camps where God dwells.
It would be better for God, being the ruler of holiness and justice, to show mercy to those who have suffered unfortunate events, rather than punishing them.
For leprosy, physical harm, and involuntary suffering happen to human bodies, but they are not considered sins.
No one chooses to be sick, and it is not right to punish those who are suffering.
If one of the wealthy were to choose to give up all his property to those who promise to deliver him from his suffering, it would be a preferable option.
The written law, which is meant to bring healing to the sick, would then be called into question.
The law's severity would be seen as a form of punishment, one that is perhaps too harsh for those who are already suffering.
The ways of the law are complex and multifaceted, and its desire to root out evil is uncontrolled, leading to a preference for the worse things in life.
The law's resemblance to leprosy is striking, for just as leprosy is a disease that affects the body, the law is a disease that affects the soul.
It is a corruption that spreads through the mind, leading to a defeat by excessive shame.
The law says that the one who is uncontrolled in lust is defiled, and this defilement is a passion that endures the suffering of uncontrolled lust.

The beauty of truth, on the other hand, is shown through a type and a shadow in the commandment given through Moses to the ancients, and the power of the things hidden in the mind is clearly shown in the bodily weaknesses.
The soul is afflicted with unyielding sorrow, a grief that has been taken on because of the dead and is deeply felt.
This sorrow is not something that can be easily shaken off, but rather it is a profound emotional response that has taken hold of the soul.
Those who are unable to control their passions and desires are not suited to be part of the community of the saints.
They are sent away, rejected because of their excessive contempt for the dead.
This contempt is a serious matter, one that is contrary to the will of God, who has made it clear through the words of the saints that the dead will rise again.
We are exhorted to be manly, to strive for virtue, and to be seen as better than our passions.
This is not an easy path, but rather one that requires effort and dedication.
The rewards, however, are great, for those who persevere will be able to possess the excellent achievements that come from a life of virtue.
It is pleasing to make an outline of our faith, with Jesus as the author and finisher, who endured the cross for the joy set before him, despising shame.
In what way and for what things he bore the cross for us, emptying himself, being God by nature, the Word, let us briefly elevate the narrative and apply it to the so-called voluntary emptying.
The Son, who is in him and from him by nature, is born from God and Father effortlessly and beyond mind.
The mind goes beyond bodies, and leaving behind the insignificant fantasy about them, it is better by far to think of the divine as incomparable to the nature of the body.
It is more excellent to consider it as having the glory of all that is generated and unblemished.

Let us accept, therefore, not necessarily following our own reasoning, that what is older than what is generated is that it does not exist at all; and somehow the non-existence appears before the transition into being.
